back: An opening in the crust through which magma, gases and fragments erupt, and the landform built around it.
Steep, tall cone of alternating ash and lava; viscous, gas-rich magma; explosive eruptions. E.g. Mount Fuji, Mount St Helens.
Broad, gently sloping volcano of runny basalt lava; frequent gentle eruptions. E.g. Mauna Loa (Hawaii).
Small, steep cone of loose cinders around one vent, often erupting only once. E.g. Parícutin (Mexico).
Active: erupted recently, likely again. Dormant: quiet for a long time but could erupt. Extinct: not expected to erupt again.
A fast (over 100 km/h), very hot avalanche of gas, ash and rock down a volcano's slopes; the deadliest hazard.
A volcanic mudflow of ash and water that travels fast down river valleys, e.g. Armero, Colombia, 1985.
A scale from 0 to 8 measuring the size of eruptions; each step is about ten times more ejected material.
Dyke: vertical sheet of igneous rock cutting across layers. Sill: horizontal sheet between layers.
Fertile soils, geothermal energy, minerals (sulphur, diamonds), tourism, new land and building stone.
